item.passage:
Transcript: Many of you play on school teams that start training in the August heat. So today I want to talk about a problem that coaches and athletes have struggled with for a long time, and about a fairly simple solution.

Here's the problem. When you exercise, your muscles produce a lot of heat. Your body gets rid of most of it by sweating. The sweat evaporates from your skin, and that cools you down. But if you've spent the summer indoors, your body isn't ready to do that well. On a hot day, your temperature can climb faster than your body can bring it down. That's when people start to feel dizzy, sick or confused, and in the worst cases, heat illness can be life-threatening. And here's the part that surprises people. Many of the serious cases happen in the first few days of practice, not in the middle of the season.

Now, you might think the answer is just to drink more water. Water matters, and you should bring a full bottle to every practice. But water alone doesn't fix this. You can drink plenty and still have a body that hasn't learned to handle the heat.

So what's the solution? It's called acclimatization. That's a long word, but it just means getting used to the heat slowly. If you exercise in warm weather a little at a time, over about ten days to two weeks, your body changes in some useful ways. First, you start sweating sooner, before you get really hot. Second, you sweat more, so you cool down better. Third, your sweat gets less salty, so you keep more of the salt your body needs. And your body holds more fluid in your blood, which means your heart doesn't have to beat as fast to do the same work.

Think of it like learning a new song on the piano. Nobody plays the whole thing perfectly on day one. You practice a bit each day, and your hands slowly figure it out. Your body learns to deal with heat in a similar way, step by step.

This year, our school's outdoor teams are going to follow this idea. The coaches all agreed to it, and honestly, I wish we'd started doing this years ago. For the first few days, practices will be shorter, about an hour, and only once a day. Players will wear light clothes, not full kit. Then each day the coaches will add a little more time and a little more effort. Only in the second week will there be longer sessions.

Some of you have told me this sounds too easy, and that real athletes should just push through. I understand that feeling, but I honestly think it's the wrong way to look at it. Going slowly at the start isn't being soft. It's what lets you train hard for the rest of the season without getting sick.

One last thing. These changes don't last forever. If you stop training in the heat for a few weeks, your body slowly loses them. So if you go away on a trip in the middle of the season, tell your coach, and you'll be eased back in.

The rain fills their tunnels with water, so they have to escape. It's a reasonable idea. I believed it myself for years. But today I want to show you why it doesn't fit the evidence, and what the other explanation is.

Let's start with how a worm breathes. A worm has no lungs. It takes in oxygen through its skin, and it can only do that while the skin is wet. In other words, water isn't the worm's enemy. It needs water to breathe. And rainwater soaking into the ground carries oxygen down with it. In fact, researchers have kept earthworms completely under water for several days, and many of them survived just fine.

The ground was soft, but there wasn't a single puddle on it. And most of the worms they counted weren't lying still. They were crawling along, some of them a long way from the grass.

So what's the other explanation? Think about how hard it is for a worm to get anywhere underground. It has to push or eat its way through the soil, a few centimetres at a time. Grass and soil stay damp much longer, so a worm crossing a lawn is fairly safe. But a worm that has crawled out into the middle of a wide path usually can't get back to the soil in time.

item.prompt: What is the lecture mainly about?
item.passage:
Transcript: So today I want to look at something you probably never think about: the little price on almost everything you buy. For most of history, there wasn't one. You and the seller argued until you agreed. That's called bargaining. To see how that changed, I'm going to use a small market town I'll call Kelbury, and the records of one shop there.

Around eighteen fifty, buying a few metres of cloth in Kelbury could take a quarter of an hour. The seller named a high price, you named a low one, and you met somewhere in the middle. If you were good at it, or well known, you paid less than your neighbour did.

Then, in eighteen seventy-two, a draper named Lorne did something unusual. A draper, by the way, is someone who sells cloth. Lorne wrote a price on a small card and pinned it to every roll of cloth in his shop, and he wrote every card himself. No more arguing. Within about thirty years, nearly every shop on Kelbury's main street had done the same.

So here's the question. Why did he do it? There are two main explanations, and I'll be honest with you, I can't tell you which one is right.

The first is fairness. With a price card, a poor customer paid exactly what a rich one paid. And Kelbury's newspaper printed a letter from a farmer's wife who loved this. She wrote that she could send her ten-year-old daughter to buy thread, and the girl would pay what the mayor paid. But notice the date. The letter is from eighteen eighty, eight years after the cards went up. So it tells us people liked fixed prices once they had them. It doesn't tell us why Lorne started.

The second explanation is about staff. Bargaining was a skill, and it took years to learn. Older shopkeepers in the town said a clerk needed about five years behind the counter before he could be trusted to bargain. The idea is that fixed prices let a shop hire people who hadn't learned that skill. Now look at Lorne's account book. In eighteen seventy-four his shop got much bigger, and he hired eight new clerks, all about fifteen years old, straight from the farms around town, for lower pay than the older clerks earned. But again, the date is a problem. Those clerks arrived two years after the cards. Maybe Lorne was planning ahead. Maybe the cards simply made the hiring possible later. The account book doesn't say.

Here's why this still matters. Today many online shops change their prices several times a day, and two people can pay different amounts for the same thing. In a way, bargaining is back, except that now only the seller does it. If fairness was the real reason prices became fixed, shoppers may push back against this. If it was mostly about running a bigger shop with cheaper staff, maybe they won't care much. Records like Kelbury's can be read either way, and historians still argue about them. Honestly, so do I.

item.prompt: How does the man feel when the woman first tells him to cut the head open?
item.passage:
Transcript: W: Hi there. Oh, is that the clay head for the art show? Put it down on the table, it looks heavy.
M: It is. It's my grandfather. I finished it last night. Could you put it in the kiln on Thursday?
W: Let me have a look. The face is lovely. But is it solid clay all the way through?
M: Yeah. I thought solid would make it stronger.
W: It's actually the opposite. Clay holds water deep inside, even when the outside feels dry. In the kiln, that water turns to steam, and if the steam can't get out, the piece can crack or even burst.
M: Burst? You mean, like, explode?
W: It happens. Last spring a solid clay apple blew apart in there. The girl who made it was really upset, and she wasn't the only one. It broke four bowls sitting next to it. Those bowls were other students' work, and they had to make them all again.
M: Oh no. So what do I do? The show's next Friday.
W: You cut the head open with a wire, scoop out the middle until the walls are about as thick as your thumb, and join it back together with soft clay. Then you poke a small hole somewhere nobody will see, under the chin maybe, so the air can escape.
M: Cut it open? It's not the work I mind. It's just, I spent three weeks on that face. The nose alone took two days. I'm scared I'll squash it.
W: You won't touch the face. We cut across the top of the head, above the ears, like a lid. I'll show you how at lunch today.
M: Couldn't I just leave it to dry for longer instead? Like, a month?
W: A month would help, but a head this thick could still be damp in the middle, and you haven't got a month. Thursday's load is all the year seven pots, so I have to be careful what goes in with them.
M: OK. Lunch today, then.
W: Good. Once it's hollow, it should dry in about five days, so we'll fire it on Tuesday. It'll be cool by Thursday, and much lighter to carry, too.
M: Lighter would be great. My grandfather's coming to see it at the show. He's never been to my school before, so I really want it there in one piece.
